Alright, the fetch_data script is now running in the background, pulling the necessary Pokémon data and sprites from the PokeAPI. While that is happening, I need to set up the basic HTML scaffold for the game so that once the assets are ready, the browser can load everything and I can start wiring up the JavaScript modules.

First, what does the final game need? At minimum, an HTML file that creates a canvas element matching the original Game Boy Advance resolution (240×160) and includes all the script files that will power the game: data files (pokedex, moves), utility modules (type chart, input handling, audio, graphics), core gameplay modules (pokemon logic, maps, UI, battle system, overworld), and the main game loop (game.js). The canvas should have an id that the rendering code can reference, and I should apply some CSS to make the canvas look pixelated (using `image-rendering: pixelated`) and give it a border reminiscent of the original handheld screen.

I also want to give the user some basic on-screen instructions for controls, because until I implement a proper menu system, a simple hint will help with testing. This can be a `<div>` below the canvas with a small monospace font and a muted color.

Now, regarding the file location: all other assets are being placed under `assets/` and JavaScript source under `js/`. The HTML file should sit at the project root (`D:\project-5\index.html`) so that relative paths resolve correctly. I need to ensure the `<script>` tags are ordered such that dependencies load before they are used: first the data files (`pokedex.js`, `moves.js`), then utility modules (`typechart.js`, `input.js`, `audio.js`, `gfx.js`), then core modules (`pokemon.js`, `maps.js`, `ui.js`, `battle.js`, `overworld.js`), and finally the entry point (`game.js`). This ordering mirrors typical module dependency graphs: data first, then helpers, then systems, then the game initializer.

I also need to set appropriate meta tags (charset, title) and basic CSS to center the canvas on the page, fill the viewport, and hide overflow. The background should be a dark color to match the original game's aesthetic.

Given all that, the content for `index.html` is straightforward. I will write the full HTML string with proper newline characters and escape any quotes as needed for the Write tool. The Write tool expects a JSON payload with `file_path` and `content`. I will set `file_path` to `D:\\project-5\\index.html` and the `content` to the HTML I just outlined, ensuring the line breaks and indentation are preserved for readability.

Now I’ll issue the Write call with these exact parameters. This will create the main entry point for the browser game, allowing me to open it later (once the data fetch completes) and start developing the JavaScript modules.
